readingInstruction: Read Psalm 118:1-18. This is the last of the Hallel psalms (113 to 118), which Jews sang at Passover and which Jesus and his disciples most likely sang at the Last Supper. Notice how often the psalm repeats “the LORD” and how the speaker moves from distress to victory.
settingTheScene: Psalm 118 is a song of thanksgiving for a national and personal deliverance, sung in procession to the temple. The speaker is a king or leader who has been surrounded by enemies and brought through. The Hallel was sung at the great feasts, and the New Testament treats this psalm as pointing to Christ: the stone the builders rejected (v. 22) and “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” (v. 26) were cried at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem. Today we read the first part, which focuses on God’s steadfast love and salvation.
observation: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
“Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free” (v. 5).
“The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (v. 6).
“It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man” (v. 8).
“All nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off!” (v. 10).
“I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me” (v. 13).
“The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation” (v. 14).
“I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The psalm begins and ends with the same words: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!” Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the LORD are called to say it. “Steadfast love” (hesed) is God’s covenant faithfulness, a love that does not let go. It is the refrain of the exodus and of the whole Old Testament. Later we will read in 1 John that “God is love,” and the two belong together. The love that endures forever is the love that sent the Son.

Then the testimony: “Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free.” The Hebrew for “set me free” is “in a broad place,” meaning out of tight distress into open space. From this the singer draws a conclusion: “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Paul takes up the same confidence in Romans 8:31: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” The LORD is my helper, and I shall look in triumph on those who hate me. Then a proverb: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.” Human help is limited; God’s help is not.

Verses 10 to 12 describe the enemies swarming like bees, flaming like a fire of thorns. Three times the singer says, “In the name of the LORD I cut them off.” Victory is not in his strength but in God’s name. Then verse 13 is honest about how close it was: “I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me.” We should not minimize the near-failure. And at the center, a line borrowed from the Song of Moses (Exodus 15:2): “The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation.” Glad songs of salvation are heard in the tents of the righteous: “The right hand of the LORD does valiantly.”

The speaker concludes this section with a statement of resurrection language: “I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD. The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.” He has been chastened but not condemned. For the singer, it is deliverance from literal death; for Christians, it points to Christ, who died and rose, and to all who are in him. He sang this psalm on the night he was betrayed, knowing what lay ahead. And the God whose love endures forever did not abandon him to the grave.
connection: Exodus 15:2 is quoted in verse 14. Psalm 56:4, 11 and Romans 8:31 echo verse 6. Jeremiah 17:5-8 contrasts trust in man and trust in the LORD. Psalm 146:3 warns against trusting princes. Matthew 26:30 and Mark 14:26 say Jesus and the disciples sang a hymn, probably the Hallel. Matthew 21:9, 42 apply verses 22 and 26 to Jesus. Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7 quote verse 22. Hebrews 12:5-11 speaks of the Lord’s discipline. 1 John 4:8-10 speaks of God’s love. 2 Corinthians 1:8-10 describes deliverance from the sentence of death.
application:
Read verse 1 aloud at the start of the day, and name three specific ways you have seen God’s steadfast love in the last week.

Name a person or institution in which you are placing too much trust. Entrust that situation to the LORD.

Memorize verse 14 as a short prayer when you feel weak.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for his steadfast love.
Thank him that the LORD is on your side.
Thank him for the stone the builders rejected.
